Within the Yazoo Basin, “recharge” of local swamps is often the result of backwater flooding from the Mississippi River proper and overbank flooding of local tributaries that drain the Basin and the adjoining Loess Hills. It is important to note that although many changes and alterations to this site have occurred, local cypress – tupelo swamps and related wetlands continue to persist. It is acknowledged that the historic conditions of this ecological site are irretrievably lost. However, if local areas continue to meet the ecological characteristics of the site’s soils (i.e., saturated conditions for much of the growing season), hydrologic regime (i.e., undrained and unmanipulated), and vegetation composition, then reference conditions within the constraints of the Yazoo Basin can be met and should be recognized. They represent the best natural or semi-natural conditions of today’s altered landscape.

text: General information - Ecoclass name: Yazoo - Wet Clayey Backswamp Flat Forest General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is representative of the broad, low backswamp flats (talfs) that developed on the periphery of and are bounded by the higher features of former and recent Mississippi River meander belts. The soils of this site coupled with their geomorphic setting are quite diagnostic and characteristic of the system. They are very deep, poorly drained and have very slow permeability. The parent material is clayey alluvium of the Mississippi River and its tributaries. Accretion and buildup of these heavy clays occur in the low, overbank environment where floodwaters become entrapped. Slopes of this site are dominantly 0 to 0.5 percent but may range up to 1 percent. This site is broadly distributed throughout the Yazoo Basin with the heaviest concentration and coverage occurring in the southern end of the basin. Of minor occurrence, the soils of this site have also been mapped on low interfluves among remnant glacial outwash channels on Late Pleistocene valley trains and swales of abandoned meander scrolls. Dominant natural vegetation of this site is often described as an overcup oak (Quercus lyrata) – water hickory (Carya aquatica) wetland forest association. Community associates include Nuttall oak (Q. texana), willow oak (Q. phellos), sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua), green ash (Fraxinus

General information - Mlra notes: The Southern Mississippi River Alluvium (MLRA 131A) is the largest of 4 MLRAs within Land Resource Region O, the Mississippi Delta Cotton and Feed Grains Region. It occurs in portions of 7 states including Louisiana (32 percent), Arkansas (26 percent), Mississippi (26 percent), Missouri (12 percent), Tennessee (3 percent), Kentucky (1 percent), and Illinois (less than 1 percent). The MLRA is comprised of 29,555 square miles and extends roughly 650 miles from an area near Cape Girardeau, Missouri in the north to the MLRA’s transition to the Gulf Coast Marsh (MLRA 151) in the south. Average elevations range from 330 feet in the north to sea level in the southern part of the area. text: The geographic distribution of all ecological sites within the Yazoo Basin is bounded to the west by an extensive, mainline levee system. Throughout its length, the constructed levee generally occurs within the current Mississippi River meander belt and is situated to the east of the active river channel. All lands between the river channel and the constructed levee are referred to as the Batture, and that subregion encapsulates its own complement of ecological sites due to significantly different hydrologic regimes (Smith and Klimas, 2002). text: Though mapped on multiple landforms, the soils, vegetation, and especially the ecological processes and functions of this site are best defined and characterized within the backswamp environment. Here, topographic relief is level with slopes dominantly at 0 to 0.5 percent but extending to 1.0 percent, locally. Various surface irregularities in this environment may include depressions of varying depths and dimensions (Berkowitz et al., 2020); low, clayey rises or ridges that range from a few inches to several feet higher than the surrounding level surfaces (Putnam and Bull, 1932); and small, low-gradient streams or sloughs that have complex interconnected flow patterns (Saucier, 1994). Floodwaters are prone to entrapment for long to very long durations due to the depressed landform being bounded by higher landscapes such as meander belts, terraces, and uplands (Smith and Klimas, 2002). Accordingly, a high water table at or slightly below ground surface persists through the wetter periods of the year, generally from winter to the growing season of spring and occasionally early summer. text: Water features - Water features: This ecological site is second only to the Frequently Flooded and Ponded Oxbow and Swale site (ID: F131AY301MS) as the wettest system in the Yazoo Basin. Next to those depressional features, this site occupies the lowest landscape position in the basin. Its level surfaces are typically bounded by higher geomorphic features creating an effective entrapment of runoff and floodwaters. Since the site occurs on the protected side of the extensive Mississippi River levee system, it may not receive overbank flooding (hydrologic recharge) on the same scale and periodicity as before the network of flood and drainage controls were constructed. Major sources of the site’s hydrology, today, are direct precipitation and backwater flooding (Smith and Klimas, 2002; Berkowitz et al., 2020). Concerning the latter, catastrophic flooding of the Mississippi River induces backwater flooding through the tributary system (via the Yazoo River) leading to inundation of the site over very long durations, particularly in the southern end of the basin. By nature of the soils and low landscape position, a high water table generally persists through the wetter periods of the year (winter and spring), especially in areas where drainage has not been drastically altered. These poorly drained soils are generally classified as hydric, and they support obligate and facultative wetland plant species and associations. Water features

text: The principal soils of this site are the Alligator (very-fine, smectitic, thermic Chromic Dystraquerts) and Sharkey (very-fine, smectitic, thermic Chromic Epiaquerts) series. Alligator soils have a light brownish gray to gray profile, are poorly drained, and formed in clayey alluvium. Average clay content of the particle size control section (10 to 40 inches) ranges from 60 to 90 percent. Reactions range from very strongly acid to slightly acid in the particle size control section. Sharkey soils have a similar drainage classification, parent material, and average clay content as that of Alligator but have a much darker profile, ranging from gray to dark gray and dark grayish brown and can be less acid, especially in the upper part of the subsoil. text: Ecological dynamics - Ecological dynamics: Historically, this ecological site was part of a vast forested landscape with processes and functions directly connected to the highly dynamic nature of the Mississippi River (Gardiner and Oliver, 2005). Today, this site is effectively disconnected from the river via the vast network of constructed levees and, in many areas, local drainage controls. Widespread changes to the landscape occurred long before any intensive studies of the historic natural communities were conducted. Accordingly, reference conditions of this ecological site are still under review. However, forest surveys conducted over the past century provide an account of tree species and forest types often associated with backswamp environments.

However, forest surveys conducted over the past century provide an account of tree species and forest types often associated with backswamp environments. The physiographic setting of this ecological site coupled with the hydrodynamics of the floodplain system contribute to the development of the soils and plant communities in this wet environment (Klimas et al., 2011). Due to flooding and ponding durations extending into the growing season, species diversity and productivity on this site are generally poor (Winters et al., 1938; Eyre, 1980; Meadows and Stanturf, 1997), and reproduction can be very sparse, especially in the wettest locations (Lentz, 1931). Putnam and Bull (1932) characterized the soils as ‘impervious clay’ and described them as “…a stiff, waxy clay that, during the fall drought, hardens to a veritable pavement.” They typified the overcup oak – water hickory type as “…practically the only one that occupies the lowest, wettest and most poorly drained, impervious clay flats.” This cover type corresponds to the Society of American Foresters (SAF) Type No. 96 (Eyre, 1980) and bears the same name. In addition to the two dominant species, associates may include Nuttall oak, willow oak, green ash, American elm, sugarberry, Drummond’s maple, cedar elm, water locust, and common persimmon (Putnam and Bull, 1932; Putnam, 1951; Eyre, 1980).

text: This ecological site is far more complex than the modal concept of level backswamp surfaces suggest. Although subtle and perhaps imperceptible, there are variability in topography and elevation within the backswamp environment and especially among the other geomorphic features of this site (i.e., remnant outwash interfluves and meander scroll swales). Just a few inches in elevation often leads to differences in drainage and the duration of flooding and ponding, and these slight differences often result in shifts in species dominance or patterns of abundance (Putnam et al., 1960). Putnam and Bull (1932) recognized these differences and included additional cover types as occurring on these level, poorly drained clayey soils. Most of the species comprising these additional types are components of the overcup oak – water hickory association, but with shorter flooding and ponding durations, reproduction and growth of these species improves. This improvement in growing conditions may give rise to one of the most desired bottomland community types in the Yazoo Basin, Putnam and Bull’s red gum (i.e., sweetgum) – clay land oaks type. This type was later absorbed into more conventional forest types such as the sweetgum – willow oak type (SAF Type No. 92; Eyre, 1980) or simply renamed the sweetgum – red oak species association (see Hodges,1997; Meadows and Stanturf, 1997). text: Putnam and Bull (1932) recognized two additional types that may be best interpreted as variations of a single association. Those two types were the oak – elm – ash and hackberry (sugarberry) – elm types. They interpreted both types as residuals following heavy cutting and removal of the best sweetgum and oaks. Today, those two types are representative of the sugarberry – American elm – green ash association (SAF Type No. 93; Eyre, 1980). This cover type has become one of the most widely distributed forest types in southern bottomland hardwood forests (Meadows and Stanturf, 1997) given the intensive land use histories most areas have incurred. Eyre (1980) provides a general description of the sugarberry – American elm – green ash type and several components listed above are associates of that type including species that are highly favored in management on this ecological site, such as Nuttall oak, willow oak, sweetgum, and green ash. Oliver et al. (2005) warns that red oaks (e.g., cherrybark, willow, water, and Nuttall) are not regrowing in sufficient concentrations to sustain their former densities, which could have consequences on other factors such as wildlife and commercial timber values. Much of these concerns are founded on forest composition transitioning to a more shade tolerant community such as the sugarberry – American elm – green ash type.

text: Overall, natural cover types on this site are minor compared to other uses. Most areas have been cleared and are used extensively for production, and many areas have been land leveled to meet irrigation needs. A secondary use on this site is pasturage. Following this narrative, a “provisional” state and transition model is provided that includes the “perceived” reference state and several alternative (or altered) vegetation states that have been observed and/or projected for this ecological site. This model is based on limited inventories, literature, expert knowledge, and interpretations. Plant communities may differ from one location to the next depending on the severity of local land use activities and rates of deposition. Depending on objectives, the reference plant community may not necessarily be the management goal.

text: General information - Ecoclass name: Yazoo - Low Clayey Backswamp Ridge Forest General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is broadly distributed in the Yazoo Basin where it occurs on multiple geomorphic settings. The site is perhaps most characteristic of slight or low ridges and rises on level, clayey backswamps. In some local flood basins, these slightly elevated and elongated rises occur in a repeated, undulating pattern with individual ridges being separated by intervening level surfaces. The site also includes linear embankments along the margins of depressions, sloughs, and former drainageways and the interfluves of remnant glacial outwash channels on Late Pleistocene valley train terraces. The soils of this site are very deep, poorly drained and have very slow permeability; parent material is clayey alluvium of the Mississippi River and its tributaries. Slopes of this site are dominantly 0.5 to 3 percent on the low ridges in backswamp environments but increase to 10 percent on remnant banks of former drainageways. Drainage improves on this elevated site compared to the adjoining level backswamps. Accordingly, diversity and productivity of the natural vegetation increases. Characteristic species of this site include Nuttall oak (Quercus texana), willow oak (Q. phellos), sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua), green ash (Fraxinus pennsylvanica), Drummond’s maple (Acer drummondii), American elm (Ulmus americana), sugarberry (Celtis laevigata), and persimmon (Diospyros virginiana). General information - Mlra notes: The Southern Mississippi River Alluvium (MLRA 131A) is the largest of 4 MLRAs within Land Resource Region O, the Mississippi Delta Cotton and Feed Grains Region. It occurs in portions of 7 states including Louisiana (32 percent), Arkansas (26 percent), Mississippi (26 percent), Missouri (12 percent), Tennessee (3 percent), Kentucky (1 percent), and Illinois (less than 1 percent). The MLRA is comprised of 29,555 square miles and extends roughly 650 miles from an area near Cape Girardeau, Missouri in the north to the MLRA’s transition to the Gulf Coast Marsh (MLRA 151) in the south. Average elevations range from 330 feet in the north to sea level in the southern part of the area. For much of the north-south distance, the MLRA is bounded to the east by an abrupt rise in elevation of loess-capped bluffs and hills, the Southern Mississippi Valley Loess (MLRA 134). text: The geographic distribution of all ecological sites within the Yazoo Basin is bounded to the west by an extensive, mainline levee system. Throughout its length, the constructed levee generally occurs within the current Mississippi River meander belt and is situated to the east of the active river channel. All lands between the river channel and the constructed levee are referred to as the Batture, and that subregion encapsulates its own complement of ecological sites due to significantly different hydrologic regimes (Smith and Klimas, 2002). text: Water features - Water features: The deep, heavy clay soils of this site are indicative of historical flooding or inundation that lasted for long to very long periods during the year. Today, this site no longer receives overland flooding (hydrologic recharge) on the same scale and periodicity as before the levees were constructed. Areas near larger tributaries of the Mississippi River flood on a far more frequent basis than do areas far removed from active and dynamic stream systems. On occasion, catastrophic flooding of the Mississippi River induces backwater flooding of the tributary systems via the Yazoo River, which can lead to inundation of the site, locally, over long periods. However, the topographic relief of this site ranges from a few inches to several feet above the surrounding flats and these low ridges and rises are the last features of the flood basin to be submerged during flood events (Putnam and Bull, 1932). In some locations, the highest ridges rarely flood. By nature of the soils and low landscape position, a high water table generally persists through the wetter periods of the year (winter and spring), especially in areas where drainage has not been drastically altered. These poorly drained soils are generally classified as hydric, and they support obligate and facultative wetland plant species and associations. Water features - Wetland

text: The principal soils of this site are the Alligator (very-fine, smectitic, thermic Chromic Dystraquerts) and Sharkey (very-fine, smectitic, thermic Chromic Epiaquerts) series. Alligator soils have a light brownish gray to gray profile, are poorly drained, and formed in clayey alluvium. Average clay content of the particle size control section (10 to 40 inches) ranges from 60 to 90 percent. Reactions range from very strongly acid to slightly acid in the particle size control section. Sharkey soils have a similar drainage classification, parent material, and average clay content as that of Alligator but have a much darker profile, ranging from gray to dark gray and dark grayish brown and can be less acid, especially in the upper part of the subsoil. text: Ecological dynamics - Ecological dynamics: Historically, this ecological site was part of a vast forested landscape with processes and functions directly connected to the highly dynamic nature of the Mississippi River (Gardiner and Oliver, 2005). Today, this site is effectively disconnected from the river via the vast network of constructed levees and, in many areas, local drainage controls. Widespread changes to the landscape occurred long before any intensive studies of the historic natural communities were conducted. Accordingly, reference conditions of this ecological site are still under review. However, observations and forest research over the past century have provided invaluable insight on species presence, suitability, and productivity of important forest resources associated with backswamp environments. That information forms the basis of the “perceived” or provisional reference state for this ecological site.

text: Although the soils are essentially the same (i.e., the Alligator and Sharkey soil series), the greater relief of this site corresponds to better drainage compared to the adjoining backswamp flats (see Provisional Ecological Site ID: F131AY302MS). Higher runoff rates and lower flooding and ponding frequencies and durations on these low ridges likely contribute to a greater diversity of natural vegetation. Putnam and McKnight (1949) mentioned that sweetgum and water oaks (i.e., willow oak, Nuttall oak, and water oak, Quercus nigra) predominate on the clayey ridges of the Delta National Forest. In an early description of forest cover types in the Mississippi River Delta Region, Putnam and Bull (1932) ranked their “red gum” (sweetgum) and “red gum – clay land oaks” cover types as “very common” associations on low clay ridges. These general cover types were later absorbed into a more conventional association by the Society of American Foresters (SAF), the sweetgum – willow oak, Type No. 92 (Eyre, 1980). A more commonly used name for the cover type is the sweetgum – red oaks association (e.g., Hodges, 1997; Meadows and Stanturf, 1997). Principal species of the community include sweetgum, Nuttall oak, willow oak, and water oak with associates of American elm, green ash, sugarberry, Drummond’s maple, cedar elm (Ulmus crassifolia), red mulberry (Morus rubra), common persimmon, and honeylocust (Gleditsia triacanthos).

text: Putnam and Bull (1932) recognized two additional types that may be best interpreted as variations of a single association. Those two types were the oak – elm – ash and hackberry (sugarberry) – elm types. They interpreted both types as residuals following heavy cutting and removal of the best sweetgum and oaks. Today, those two general types are included in the sugarberry – American elm – green ash association (SAF Type No. 93; Eyre, 1980). This cover type has become one of the most widely distributed forest types in southern bottomland hardwood forests (Meadows and Stanturf, 1997) given the intensive land use histories most areas have incurred. However, Hodges (1997) emphasized that most successional pathways on poorly drained sites in major bottoms tend toward this association, and that pathway also includes the potential fate of the sweetgum – red oaks type. The principal species of the sugarberry – elm – ash association are prolific seed producers and are shade tolerant when young. These biological attributes give them a competitive edge over their oak associates, which are shade intolerant, have poor seedling establishment under high shade, and have slow early growth (Eyre, 1980). Hodges (1997) emphasized that the sugarberry – elm – ash cover type is long-lived and capable of self-replacement. Still, there are potential natural events and management scenarios that may favor development of the sweetgum – red oaks community. These factors ultimately depend on disturbance (e.g., a catastrophic stand replacing event) and the presence of advance regeneration within the stand prior to disturbance. Under the disturbance scenario, the presence of advance regeneration of oaks may favor establishment of the sweetgum – red oak association following a stand replacing event. Although, in the absence of large-scale disturbances, the long-term trend favors the development and persistence of the shade tolerant, sugarberry – elm – ash cover type (Hodges, 1997; Stanturf et al., 2001).

text: Overall, natural cover types on this site are minor compared to other uses. Most areas have been cleared and are used extensively for production, and many areas have been land leveled to meet irrigation needs. A secondary use on this site is pasturage. Wetness limitations on this site have led to the installation of drainage systems in many areas. Following this narrative, a “provisional” state and transition model is provided that includes the “perceived” reference state and several alternative (or altered) vegetation states that have been observed and/or projected for this ecological site. This model is based on limited inventories, literature, expert knowledge, and interpretations. Plant communities may differ from one location to the next depending on the severity of local land use activities and rates of deposition. text: General information - Ecoclass name: Yazoo - Wet Transitional Backswamp Forest General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site mainly functions as a transitional bridge between the toe and lower backslopes of recent natural levees to the low backswamp environments of the floodplain. Hence, the site’s distribution in the Yazoo Basin primarily occurs within and along the periphery of the more recent Mississippi River meander belt and is heavily influenced by trapped backwater during flood events. Secondarily, the site occurs locally within the flood basins of active Mississippi River tributaries and the distributary, Deer Creek. The soils of this site are poorly drained to somewhat poorly drained that formed in recent clayey and clayey over loamy alluvium. The reaction class of these soils is nonacid, and permeability through the clayey upper layers is very slow but increases to moderate in the loamy lower horizon(s), where present. Slopes are dominantly 0 to 3 percent but range to 5 percent; the higher slope percentages occur on low, narrow ridges and rises within the flood basin. Flooding typically occurs in winter to early spring with durations that can last from a few days to several weeks depending on flood severity and proximity to flood source. Associates of occasional occurrence include cherrybark oak (Q. pagoda) and pecan (Cara illinoinensis) on drier locations and overcup oak (Q. lyrata) and water hickory (C. aquatica) in areas that remain saturated for longer periods. Dominance patterns are likely to vary tremendously with respect to location, and the prevailing forest type in some areas may be the sugarberry – American elm – green ash association. Former and current land use practices, local drainage patterns, and proximity to other community types, among other factors, contribute to species variability on this site. Most areas, today, are cleared and under various forms of agriculture production. text: Alluvium (MLRA 131A) is the largest of 4 MLRAs within Land Resource Region O, the Mississippi Delta Cotton and Feed Grains Region. It occurs in portions of 7 states including Louisiana (32 percent), Arkansas (26 percent), Mississippi (26 percent), Missouri (12 percent), Tennessee (3 percent), Kentucky (1 percent), and Illinois (less than 1 percent). The MLRA is comprised of 29,555 square miles and extends roughly 650 miles from an area near Cape Girardeau, Missouri in the north to the MLRA’s transition to the Gulf Coast Marsh (MLRA 151) in the south. Average elevations range from 330 feet in the north to sea level in the southern part of the area. For much of the north-south distance, the MLRA is bounded to the east by an abrupt rise in elevation of loess-capped bluffs and hills, the Southern Mississippi Valley Loess (MLRA 134). West of the Mississippi River, the boundary is less distinct except to the northwest where the MLRA abuts the Ozark Plateaus and Ouachita province (MLRAs 116A, 117, and 118A). South of the Ozark and Ouachita escarpment, the MLRA adjoins the Southern Mississippi River Terraces (MLRA 131D), which includes the fabled Grand Prairie and merges with the valleys of the Arkansas and Ouachita rivers (MLRA 131B) and the Red River (MLRA 131C). text: The geographic distribution of all ecological sites within the Yazoo Basin is bounded to the west by an extensive, mainline levee system. Throughout its length, the constructed levee generally occurs within the current Mississippi River meander belt and is situated to the east of the active river channel. All lands between the river channel and the constructed levee are referred to as the Batture, and that subregion encapsulates its own complement of ecological sites due to significantly different hydrologic regimes (Smith and Klimas, 2002). text: Physiographic features - Physiographic features: This ecological site’s distribution in the Yazoo Basin primarily occurs within and along the periphery of the more recent Mississippi River meander belt. The site mainly functions as a transitional bridge between the toe and lower backslopes of recent natural levees and the low backswamp environments of the floodplain. This transitional bridge between the natural levee and the backswamp occurred during the shifting of the Mississippi River channel within the meander belt. Elevation and landscape position of these soils are slightly lower than the Recent Wet Natural Levee and Meander Scroll (F131AY312MS) site (dominantly Bowdre and Mhoon soils) but are slightly higher than the adjoining Wet Clayey Backswamp Flat (F131AY302MS) where Sharkey and Alligator soils are dominant. Hence, this site grades from the diverse and complex recent natural levees to the wet flood basin of the Mississippi River Alluvium. Secondarily, the soils of this site are mapped locally on meander scroll swales and along the flood basins of active Mississippi River tributaries (e.g., Big Sunflower River) and the distributary, Deer Creek.

text: Water features - Water features: This site occurs in a variety of water receiving positions. It’s primary distribution and function is that it forms a bridge between the wet toeslopes of recent natural levees and the low, clayey flats (or talfs) of the flood basin. Secondarily, the soils of this site are mapped locally along or near active tributaries, a major distributary, and on some meander scroll swales. The soils are heavily influenced by precipitation, a high water table, and are subject to occasional overland flow and backwater flooding. Today, this site occurs on the protected side of an extensive levee system and no longer receives overland flooding on the same scale that it may have experienced prior to levee construction. Locations that may continue to flood on any predictable basis are typically restricted to stream corridors and other low features (e.g., depressions) that receive overland flow or backwater flooding. Notably, the seasonal high water table and somewhat poorly to poorly drained soils of this site provide suitable conditions for some obligate and facultative wetland plants. However, many soils or soil map unit components associated with this site may not meet hydric soil criteria (Kirchner et al., 1992), but some may. Caution is warranted when attempting offsite wetland determinations. Water features - Wetland description: Under the Cowardin et al. (1979)

This site is characterized by very deep, somewhat poorly drained and poorly drained soils that formed in recent clayey and clayey over loamy Mississippi River alluvium. Slopes are dominantly 0 to 3 percent but may range upward to 5 and 7 percent on low, narrow ridges or rises. Depending on location, landuse history, and soil horizon, reactions generally range from moderately acid to moderately alkaline. The available water capacity is high; organic matter content is moderate; and natural fertility is high. The clayey horizons of these soils have a high shrink-swell potential and permeability is very slow. Permeability improves and generally increases to moderate in the loamy horizons of those soils that have a loamy subsoil below the clayey horizons. These soils are episaturated in the surface layer and along cracks and slickensides in the upper subsoil during the wetter periods of winter into early spring. All underlying layers are wet.

text: Ecological dynamics - Ecological dynamics: Historically, this ecological site was part of a vast forested landscape with processes and functions directly connected to the highly dynamic nature of the Mississippi River (Gardiner and Oliver, 2005). Today, this site is effectively disconnected from the river via the vast network of constructed levees and, in many areas, local drainage controls. Widespread changes to the landscape occurred long before any intensive studies of the historic natural communities were conducted. Accordingly, reference conditions of this ecological site are still under review.

text: in many areas, local drainage controls. Widespread changes to the landscape occurred long before any intensive studies of the historic natural communities were conducted. Accordingly, reference conditions of this ecological site are still under review. The soils of this site are often associated and grouped with other clayey soils of backswamp or “slackwater” environments, such as the Sharkey and Alligator soil series. However, this ecological site is positioned a little higher in elevation, and the loamy subsoils, where present, have better internal drainage than the very deep, heavy clays of either Sharkey or Alligator soils. Although mapped in a variety of floodplain settings, a characteristic occurrence (or distribution) of these clayey over loamy soils is along the lower and wetter periphery of recent natural levees where they typically extend to the lower and much wetter backswamps, often adjoining Sharkey soils (USDA-SCS, 1958; USDA-SCS, 1961). This ecological site forms a soil and vegetation gradient or transition from the higher riverfront hardwoods of the recent natural levees and point bars to the low, overcup oak – water hickory community of the wet, clayey backswamps (see Ecological Site ID F131AY302MS).

text: gradient or transition from the higher riverfront hardwoods of the recent natural levees and point bars to the low, overcup oak – water hickory community of the wet, clayey backswamps (see Ecological Site ID F131AY302MS). Species occurring on this site consist of a mix of riverfront hardwoods that are tolerant of wet conditions in addition to components that typically occur in low backswamp environments. Tree species listed as frequently occurring on the dominant soils of this site include sweetgum, Nuttall oak, water oak, willow oak, American elm, sugarberry, and red maple. Associates or species occasionally occurring include green ash, eastern cottonwood, cherrybark oak, Shumard's oak (Quercus shumardii), pecan, common persimmon, American sycamore, cedar elm, and black willow (Broadfoot and McKnight, 1961; Broadfoot, 1976). The wettest locations may support occasional occurrences of overcup oak and water hickory (Broadfoot and McKnight, 1961).

text: General information - Ecoclass name: Yazoo - Old Sandy Natural Levee and Meander Scroll Ridge Forest General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site consists entirely of sandy soils that were deposited during historic flood events. These deep, coarse-textured soils occur on older natural levees and meander scroll ridges that border former channels and courses of the Mississippi River. Additionally, the soils of this site have been mapped along larger, active channels and bayous – all tributaries to the Mississippi River. Soils are very deep, excessively to somewhat excessively drained that formed in loamy or sandy alluvium. Slopes range from 0 to 8 percent. The soils of this site differ from recently deposited materials in that they are much older, more weathered, and have reactions that can be slightly to strongly acid. Some locations have been abandoned by the parent stream for millennia. Under natural conditions, the plant communities of this site likely vary widely depending on past disturbances, stage of natural succession, and the degree of periodic flooding. There is some suggestion that areas of little disturbance over very long periods of time may succeed to an oak – hickory climax. text: Sunflower River, Bogue Phalia, and the distributary Deer Creek), all flow to the only significant outlet for the basin, the Yazoo River, which enters the Mississippi River near Vicksburg (Saucier, 1994; Klimas et al., 2011). Historically, large floods on the Mississippi River and in the Yazoo tributary system inundated most, if not all, of the Yazoo Basin (Moore, 1972). These periodic floods and the ponding aftereffects oftentimes lasted for very long durations (Berkowitz et al., 2020), delivering nutrient-rich sediments that were critical to the production and maintenance of the dominant natural vegetation, bottomland hardwood forests (Taylor et al., 1990; MMNS, 2015). Since settlement, the biophysical environment of the area has been vastly altered. Perhaps the most notable change entails extensive modification of the basin’s natural hydrology, which includes hundreds of miles of constructed levees along the mainstem of the Mississippi River and basin tributaries; channel modifications on many streams; water control structures; land leveled areas; and an extensive network of surface drainage systems (Kirchner et al., 1992). Even with these measures, widespread backwater flooding occurs in the southern portion of the area (Yazoo Backwater Area) when high stages are reached on the Mississippi River. The extensive modifications to the basin’s hydrology coupled with increased access (Hudson, 1979) set the stage for broadscale conversion of former forestland to a variety of land uses with agriculture production being dominant. Today, bottomland hardwood forests cover roughly 10 percent of the original forest area (Smith and Klimas, 2002).

text: The geographic distribution of all ecological sites within the Yazoo Basin is bounded to the west by an extensive, mainline levee system. Throughout its length, the constructed levee generally occurs within the current Mississippi River meander belt and is situated to the east of the active river channel. All lands between the river channel and the constructed levee are referred to as the Batture, and that subregion encapsulates its own complement of ecological sites due to significantly different hydrologic regimes (Smith and Klimas, 2002). text: Physiographic features - Physiographic features: This ecological site is broadly mapped in the Yazoo Basin. It primarily occupies the highest positions of old natural levees and meander scroll ridges that border former channels of the Mississippi River. Secondarily, the soils of this site are mapped sporadically on natural levees and stream corridors of active tributaries to the Mississippi River. On some landforms, such as former meander scrolls, the terrain may undertake a gently undulating pattern – the characteristic “ridge and swale” topography – with the soils of this site occupying the highest positions. text: Water features - Water features: This site occupies the highest positions of old natural levees and meander scroll ridges. The location or position of this site is high enough in elevation that it does not flood on a frequent or predictable basis. text: Commonly mapped soils of this site consist of the Beulah (coarse-loamy, mixed, active, thermic Typic Dystrudepts) series and the inactive Clack series. Beulah soils are somewhat excessively drained, have moderately rapid permeability, and have a cambic horizon from 8 to 28 inches (Bw1 and Bw2) below the surface. The Clack soils were described as excessively drained, having surface textures that ranged from fine sandy loam to loamy sand, and having reactions that ranged from moderately to strongly acid. Where the Clack soils were mapped, later assessments indicated that the Bruno (sandy, mixed, thermic Typic Udifluvents) series were a better fit. Bruno soils are also excessively drained, have rapid permeability, and formed in sandy alluvium and thin strata of finer textures. text: Ecological dynamics - Ecological dynamics: Historically, this ecological site was part of a vast forested landscape with processes and functions directly connected to the highly dynamic nature of the Mississippi River (Gardiner and Oliver, 2005). Today, this site is effectively disconnected from the Mississippi River via the vast network of constructed levees and, in many areas, local drainage controls. Widespread changes to the landscape occurred long before any intensive studies of the historic natural communities were conducted. Accordingly, reference conditions of this ecological site are still under review and consideration. This site was created by heavy deposition of coarse material during historical storm events. The soils of this site represent old crevasse or sand splays that were deposited many years ago. These older alluvial soils are typically distinguished from their younger counterparts by having reactions that are moderately to strongly acid and by containing strata of finer sediments.

These older alluvial soils are typically distinguished from their younger counterparts by having reactions that are moderately to strongly acid and by containing strata of finer sediments. Plant communities associated with this site underwent dramatic changes over time. When these soils were first deposited, early colonizers were likely cottonwood (Populus deltoides) and black willow (Salix nigra) or possibly sandbar willow (Salix interior) if associated with sand bars and accreting point bars. These were later replaced by the riverfront forest association (Meadows and Nowacki, 1996), which likely consisted of components of the American sycamore – pecan – American elm type, a variant of the American sycamore – sweetgum – American elm type (Society of American Foresters, SAF, Type No. 94; Eyre, 1980). As the site aged, locations experiencing little disturbance may have succeeded to a longer-lived, resilient system that consisted of a complex mixture of southern hardwoods including proportionally more oaks and hickory. Once locations became abandoned by the river and active accretion halted altogether, plant succession continued to influence the composition of this dry, sandy site. There is some suggestion that areas of little disturbance over very long periods of time may succeed to an oak – hickory climax (Putnam and Bull, 1932; Shelford, 1954; Hodges, 1997).

Utilizing the description of forest types from Putnam (1951), the soil survey manuscript of Sunflower County, Mississippi (USDA-SCS, 1959) indicated Putnam’s “white oaks – red oaks – other hardwoods” type as occurring on “…coarser textured soils of the old natural levees.” That association in the survey manuscript suggests that Putnam’s forest type, or some components of the type, may be shared between this site and the adjoining Old Loamy Natural Levee and Meander Scroll Ridge Forest (F131AY306MS). Putnam (1951) described the type as occurring best on “…fine sandy loam soils on first bottom ridges and all ridges on the terraces.” The typical pedon described for Beulah soils is very fine sandy loam (USDA-NRCS-SSS, 2017). Many of the species that Putnam listed as important components of his white oaks – red oaks – other hardwoods type may be important components of this site. In locations where the soils are sandier, components more tolerant of droughty conditions may dominate, such as bottomland post oak (locally known as Delta post oak), white oak, southern red oak, sweetgum, hickory, blackgum, and winged elm (Ulmus alata). Species that may occur in greater abundance on loamy (or less sandy) locations, in addition to the preceding, may include cherrybark oak, water oak, sugarberry, and American elm (Ulmus americana) (Sharitz and Mitsch, 1993).

text: General information - Ecoclass name: Yazoo - Old Loamy Natural Levee and Meander Scroll Ridge Forest General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is broadly distributed in the Yazoo Basin where it primarily occurs on the higher positions of older natural levees and meander scroll ridges that borders former channels of the Mississippi River. Secondarily, the soils of this site are mapped sporadically on natural levees of active Mississippi River tributaries and the distributary, Deer Creek and on higher interfluves of remnant glacial outwash channels on Late Pleistocene valley train terraces. Slopes associated with the higher positions of this site generally range from 0 to 8 percent. Soils are very deep, well drained to moderately well drained that formed in loamy alluvium. A key characteristic of these soils is the prominent profile development as determined by distinct argillic (clay) accumulations in the subsoil (B horizon). Soil reactions generally range from very strongly acid to moderately acid. The higher, drier soils of this group are quite productive and support a broad range of species including water oak (Quercus nigra), swamp chestnut oak (Q. michauxii), cherrybark oak (Q pagoda), bottomland post oak (Q. similis), Shumard’s oak (Q. shumardii), hickory (Carya spp.), blackgum (Nyssa sylvatica), and winged elm (Ulmus alata). General information - Mlra notes: The Southern Mississippi River Alluvium (MLRA 131A) is the largest of 4 MLRAs within Land Resource Region O, the Mississippi Delta Cotton and Feed Grains Region. It occurs in portions of 7 states including Louisiana (32 percent), Arkansas (26 percent), Mississippi (26 percent), Missouri (12 percent), Tennessee (3 percent), Kentucky (1 percent), and Illinois (less than 1 percent). The MLRA is comprised of 29,555 square miles and extends roughly 650 miles from an area near Cape Girardeau, Missouri in the north to the MLRA’s transition to the Gulf Coast Marsh (MLRA 151) in the south. Average elevations range from 330 feet in the north to sea level in the southern part of the area. For much of the north-south distance, the MLRA is bounded to the east by an abrupt rise in elevation of loess-capped bluffs and hills, the Southern Mississippi Valley Loess (MLRA 134). text: The geographic distribution of all ecological sites within the Yazoo Basin is bounded to the west by an extensive, mainline levee system. Throughout its length, the constructed levee generally occurs within the current Mississippi River meander belt and is situated to the east of the active river channel. text: Water features - Water features: This site occurs on the highest positions of old natural levees, meander scroll ridges, and interfluves among remnant outwash channels. Today, this site occurs on the protected side of the extensive Mississippi River levee system and no longer receives overland flooding on the same scale that it may have experienced prior to levee construction. For the most part, the location or position of this site is high enough in elevation that it does not flood on a frequent or predictable basis. In general, this site does not support wetland species and does not qualify as supporting hydric conditions or meeting “wetland determination” criteria.

This site is characterized by very deep, well drained and moderately well drained soils that formed in loamy alluvium. A key characteristic of these soils is the prominent profile development as determined by distinct argillic (clay) accumulations in the subsoil (B horizon). Soil reactions generally range from very strongly acid to moderately acid. Slopes associated with the higher positions of this site generally range from 0 to 8 percent. Several different soil series comprise this site including both active and one inactive series. The dominant soils of the site are the Dubbs (fine-silty, mixed, active, thermic Typic Hapludalfs) series. Dubbs soils are well drained and have base saturation (by sum of cations) from 65 to 80 percent at depths of 50 inches below the upper boundary of the B horizon.

Dubbs soils are well drained and have base saturation (by sum of cations) from 65 to 80 percent at depths of 50 inches below the upper boundary of the B horizon. The next most commonly mapped soils of the site are the Bosket (fine-loamy, mixed, active, thermic Mollic Hapludalfs) series. Bosket soils are well drained and have a mollic epipedon. However, many areas that were mapped Bosket may no longer support the mollic surface layer either due to erosion and detrimental landuse practices or to landleveling. Some areas formerly mapped Bosket may in fact be Teksob (fine-loamy, mixed, active, thermic Typic Hapludalfs) soils due to loss of the mollic epipedon of Bosket soils (R. Stout-Evans, personal communication). Teksob soils are well drained with surface textures of fine sandy loam, sandy loam, or loam. Additional soils include the Askew (fine-silty, mixed, active, thermic Aquic Hapludalfs), Dexter (fine-silty, mixed, active, thermic Ultic Hapludalfs), and Tutwiler (coarse-silty, mixed, active, thermic Typic Hapludalfs) series. Askew soils are moderately well drained with a perched water table at a depth of 2 to 3 feet during winter to early spring in most years (USDA-NRCS, 2006b). Dexter soils are well drained and in a fine-silty family – contrasting with Tutwiler soils, which are coarse-silty.

text: areas, local drainage controls. Widespread changes to the landscape occurred long before any intensive studies of the historic natural communities were conducted. Accordingly, reference conditions of this ecological site are still under review and consideration. Utilizing the description of forest types from Putnam (1951), the soil survey manuscript of Sunflower County, Mississippi (USDA-SCS, 1959) indicated that Putnam’s “white oaks – red oaks – other hardwoods” type as occurring on “…coarser textured soils of the old natural levees.” That association in the survey manuscript suggests that Putnam’s forest type either occurs solely on this site or shares forest components with the adjoining Old Sandy Natural Levee and Meander Scroll Ridge Forest (site ID: F131AY305MS). Important or key species comprising the type include swamp chestnut oak, white oak, bottomland post oak (known locally as Delta post oak), cherrybark oak, Shumard’s oak, southern red oak, white ash, hickory, blackgum, and winged elm (Putnam, 1951). Additional forest associates that are important components in some locations include sweetgum, water oak, willow oak, and American elm (Eyre, 1980; MMNS, 2015). Putnam (1951) added that this association produces some of the highest valued species and products among the southern bottomland forest types.

Components and/or variants of other forest types such as the sweetgum – red oaks and the elm – ash – sugarberry associations (see Meadows and Stanturf, 1997 for brief descriptions) may converge on this site forming complex species patterns (Hodges, 1995). Such complexities may also be due to former landuse histories in addition to contrasting soil-site environments being juxtaposed. Overall, forest cover on this site is minor compared to other uses. Most areas have been cleared and are used extensively for row crop production. Some areas have been land leveled to meet irrigation needs. A secondary use on this site is pasturage.

text: General information - Ecoclass name: Yazoo - Old Moderately Wet Natural Levee and Meander Scroll Ridge Forest General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is broadly distributed in the Yazoo Basin where it is generally associated with older meander belts (former channels) of the Mississippi River and its distributaries. The site occupies positions intermediate to the higher, better drained areas and the lower, wetter toeslopes of former natural levees and meander scroll ridges. Additionally, the soils of this site have been mapped along active tributaries to the Mississippi River, on low ridges and rises adjacent to backswamp areas, and on interfluves of remnant glacial outwash channels. The soils are very deep, somewhat poorly drained that formed in thinly stratified beds of loamy alluvium. A key characteristic of these soils is the prominent profile development as determined by distinct argillic (clay) accumulations in the subsoil (B horizon). Slopes are typically 0 to 3 percent but may range up to 8 percent. Under natural drainage conditions, an apparent water table occurs 1.5 to 3.5 feet below the surface during the winter and spring months in most years. In areas that are intentionally drained, the water table ranges from 3.5 to 6 feet below the surface. Average elevations range from 330 feet in the north to sea level in the southern part of the area. For much of the north-south distance, the MLRA is bounded to the east by an abrupt rise in elevation of loess-capped bluffs and hills, the Southern Mississippi Valley Loess (MLRA 134). West of the Mississippi River, the boundary is less distinct except to the northwest where the MLRA abuts the Ozark Plateaus and Ouachita province (MLRAs 116A, 117, and 118A). South of the Ozark and Ouachita escarpment, the MLRA adjoins the Southern Mississippi River Terraces (MLRA 131D), which includes the fabled Grand Prairie and merges with the valleys of the Arkansas and Ouachita rivers (MLRA 131B) and the Red River (MLRA 131C). Occurring within or bordering the Southern Mississippi River Alluvium are three separate loess-capped, upland remnants: Crowley’s Ridge, Macon Ridge, and Lafayette Loess Plain, which are western units of MLRA 134 (USDA-NRCS, 2006a).

text: The geographic distribution of all ecological sites within the Yazoo Basin is bounded to the west by an extensive, mainline levee system. text: Water features - Water features: This site occurs in a variety of alluvial plain settings that include mid-slope positions of old or former natural levees and meander scroll ridges; the margins of backswamp environments; broad interfluves among remnant outwash channels; and the margins of active streams and tributaries to the Mississippi River. Today, this site occurs on the protected side of the extensive Mississippi River levee system and no longer receives overland flooding on the same scale that it may have experienced prior to levee construction. For the most part, the location or position of this site is high enough in elevation that it does not flood on a frequent or predictable basis. The locations that may continue to flood on any predictable basis are typically restricted to stream margins or adjacent to other depressional features that may receive overland flow or backwater flooding. In general, this site does not support wetland obligate species, although facultative wetland species may be present on any given location. This site does not qualify as supporting hydric conditions or meeting “wetland determination” criteria.

This site is characterized by very deep, somewhat poorly drained soils that formed in loamy alluvium. The dominant and most important soils of this site are the Dundee (fine-silty, mixed, active, thermic Typic Endoaqualfs) series. The site’s core concepts and spatial distribution in the Yazoo Basin are based largely on the characteristics and mapped distribution of these soils. A key characteristic of these soils is the prominent profile development as determined by distinct argillic (clay) accumulations in the subsoil (B horizon). Slopes are typically 0 to 3 percent but may range up to 8 percent. Under natural drainage conditions, an apparent water table occurs 1.5 to 3.5 feet below the surface during the winter and spring months in most years. In areas that are intentionally drained, the water table ranges from 3.5 to 6 feet below the surface.

text: Secondary soils of this site are represented by an inactive series, the Pearson series. These soils were historically mapped in several counties within the Yazoo Basin and were generally described as having been formed in silty alluvium with reactions that ranges from strongly to moderately acid. However, drainage characteristics were sometimes broadly described as being moderately well drained to somewhat poorly drained (USDA-SCS, 1958; USDA-SCS, 1961). Recent transect pedons revealed that most areas where the soils were mapped on natural levees best fit the established Dubbs soil series (see Yazoo – Old Loamy Natural Levee and Meander Scroll Ridge Forest, PES ID F131AY306MS). The exception are the Pearson soils that were mapped in the county where the series was established, Quitman County, Mississippi. Field investigations indicate that the Pearson soils in Quitman County have a poorer drainage than most pedons elsewhere and are best grouped with the somewhat poorly drained Dundee soils of this site. text: areas, local drainage controls. Widespread changes to the landscape occurred long before any intensive studies of the historic natural communities were conducted. Accordingly, reference conditions of this ecological site are still under review and consideration. Putnam and Bull (1932) described their willow oak – cherrybark oak – cow oak (swamp chestnut oak) type as having characteristics of soil, moisture, and elevation midway or intermediate to the “typical flats and typical ridges.” They also mentioned the type occurring on undulating topography with a mixture of flat and ridge conditions. It can’t be assumed that the authors were describing or “typing” this ecological site without further investigation. However, their general descriptions of the landscape position and characteristics of that association are similar to the geomorphic features of this soil-site environment. Dominant components of their type include willow oak, cherrybark oak, swamp chestnut oak, Nuttall oak, and water oak with associates of sweetgum, American elm (Ulmus americana), green ash, persimmon, and sugarberry (Celtis laevigata). They emphasized that much variation occurred among and between stands with respect to sub-types, species dominance, co-dominance, and even presence/absence of some components.

text: Overall, forest cover on this site is minor compared to other uses. Most areas have been cleared and are used for growing cotton, corn, soybeans, and small grain. This site is used extensively for row crop production and some areas have been land leveled up to 3 feet to meet irrigation needs. A secondary use on this site is pasturage. Following this narrative, a “provisional” state and transition model is provided that includes the “perceived” reference state and several alternative (or altered) vegetation states that have been observed and/or projected for this ecological site. This model is based on limited inventories, literature, expert knowledge, and interpretations. Plant communities may differ from one location to the next depending on the severity of local land use activities and rates of deposition. Depending on objectives, the reference plant community may not necessarily be the management goal.

text: General information - Ecoclass name: Yazoo - Old Wet Natural Levee and Meander Scroll Forest General information - Ecoclass concept: This ecological site is broadly distributed in the Yazoo Basin where it is generally associated with older meander belts (former channels) of the Mississippi River and its tributaries. Within the meander belt environment, the site occupies the lowest and wettest position on old natural levees and low, narrow rises and flats on meander scrolls. Additionally, the soils of this site have been mapped on higher flats and gently sloping areas that grade to adjoining backswamps and on interfluves of remnant glacial outwash channels of Pleistocene-age valley train terraces. The site consists of very deep, somewhat poorly drained and poorly drained soils that formed in clayey, clayey over loamy, and silty alluvium. A key characteristic of these soils is the prominent profile development as determined by distinct argillic (clay) accumulations in the subsoil (B horizon). Slopes are typically 0 to 3 percent but may range up to 8 percent. Under natural drainage conditions, an apparent water table occurs 0.5 to 2.0 feet below the surface during the winter and spring months in most years. Natural vegetation of this site, today, is directly influenced by former landuse activities at varying intensity levels. Canopy species reported as frequently occurring and favored in management

text: The Southern Mississippi River Alluvium (MLRA 131A) is the largest of 4 MLRAs within Land Resource Region O, the Mississippi Delta Cotton and Feed Grains Region. It occurs in portions of 7 states including Louisiana (32 percent), Arkansas (26 percent), Mississippi (26 percent), Missouri (12 percent), Tennessee (3 percent), Kentucky (1 percent), and Illinois (less than 1 percent). The MLRA is comprised of 29,555 square miles and extends roughly 650 miles from an area near Cape Girardeau, Missouri in the north to the MLRA’s transition to the Gulf Coast Marsh (MLRA 151) in the south. Average elevations range from 330 feet in the north to sea level in the southern part of the area. For much of the north-south distance, the MLRA is bounded to the east by an abrupt rise in elevation of loess-capped bluffs and hills, the Southern Mississippi Valley Loess (MLRA 134). West of the Mississippi River, the boundary is less distinct except to the northwest where the MLRA abuts the Ozark Plateaus and Ouachita province (MLRAs 116A, 117, and 118A). South of the Ozark and Ouachita escarpment, the MLRA adjoins the Southern Mississippi River Terraces (MLRA 131D), which includes the fabled Grand Prairie and merges with the valleys of the Arkansas and Ouachita rivers (MLRA 131B) and the Red River (MLRA 131C). Water features - Water features: This site occurs on a variety of water receiving positions, including toe slopes of former natural levees; flats (talfs) and low rises on former meander scrolls; margins of backswamp environments; and broad interfluves among remnant outwash channels. Today, this site occurs on the protected side of the extensive Mississippi River levee system and no longer receives overland flooding on the same scale that it may have experienced prior to levee construction. The locations that continue to flood on any predictable basis are generally restricted to stream margins or other low features (e.g., depressions) that receive overland flow or backwater flooding. The period of greatest flood potential is late winter through early spring. Under natural drainage conditions, an apparent water table occurs 0.5 to 2.0 feet below the surface during the winter and spring months in most years. The seasonal high water table and poorly drained soils of this site provide suitable conditions for wetland obligate and facultative wetland plants. This site is influenced by local hydrologic regimes.
Water features - Wetland description: Under the Cowardin et al. (1979) system, this site is classified as:
System: Palustrine
Class: Forested Wetland
Subclass: Broad-leaved Deciduous

This site consists of very deep, somewhat poorly drained and poorly drained soils that formed in clayey, clayey over loamy, and silty alluvium. A key characteristic of these soils is the prominent profile development as determined by distinct argillic (clay) accumulations in the subsoil (B horizon), which differ from the catena of soils (Entisols and Inceptisols) on current or recent Mississippi River meander belts. The dominant and most important soils of this site are the Forestdale (fine, smectitic, thermic Typic Endoaqualfs) series. This site’s core concepts and spatial distribution in the Yazoo Basin are based largely on the characteristics and mapped distribution of these soils. Forestdale soils formed in clayey and silty alluvium, are poorly drained, and have very slow permeability.

text: Secondary soils of this site are the Tensas (fine, smectitic, thermic Chromic Vertic Epiaqualfs) series and the inactive series Brittain. Tensas soils formed in clayey over loamy alluvium, are somewhat poorly drained, and have very slow permeability. The Brittain series was recognized as having formed in silty materials on stream terraces. Its principal topographic or physiographic profile was described as being slightly depressional to gently sloping with slow surface drainage and poor internal drainage. Some of the early soil surveys within the Yazoo Basin mapped Brittain soils on old natural levees (e.g., USDA-SCS, 1958; USDA-SCS, 1959). text: Ecological dynamics - Ecological dynamics: Historically, this ecological site was part of a vast forested landscape with processes and functions directly connected to the highly dynamic nature of the Mississippi River (Gardiner and Oliver, 2005). Today, this site is effectively disconnected from the Mississippi River via the vast network of constructed levees and, in many areas, local drainage controls. Widespread changes to the landscape occurred long before any intensive studies of the natural communities were conducted. Accordingly, reference conditions of this ecological site are still under review and consideration.

Accordingly, reference conditions of this ecological site are still under review and consideration. Utilizing the description of forest types from Putnam (1951), the soil survey manuscript of Sunflower County, Mississippi (USDA-SCS, 1959) indicated that Putnam’s “sweetgum – water oaks” forest type as occurring on “...level and nearly level old natural levees.” Thus, the soil survey manuscript associates or deems that forest type as representative of this ecological site. Important or key species comprising the type include sweetgum, water oak, Nuttall oak, willow oak, American elm, sugarberry, and green ash. Additional forest associates include overcup oak, pecan, water hickory, cedar elm, eastern cottonwood, laurel oak, red maple, honeylocust (Gleditsia triacanthos), and persimmon (Putnam, 1951). Putnam indicated that variations of the sweetgum – water oaks type were commonplace with variants comprised predominantly of either sweetgum, water oaks (i.e., Nuttall, willow, water, and overcup), or a third variant, the cedar elm – water oaks forest type.

text: Overall, forest cover on this site is minor compared to other uses. Most areas have been cleared and are used extensively for row crop production. Some areas have been land leveled to meet irrigation needs. A secondary use on this site is pasturage. Wetness limitations have prompted many to install drainage systems. Following this narrative, a “provisional” state and transition model is provided that includes the “perceived” reference state and several alternative (or altered) vegetation states that have been observed and/or projected for this ecological site. This model is based on limited inventories, literature, expert knowledge, and interpretations. Plant communities may differ from one location to the next depending on the severity of local land use activities and rates of deposition. Depending on objectives, the reference plant community may not necessarily be the management goal.

text: General information - Ecoclass name: Yazoo - Recent Sandy Natural Levee and Meander Scroll Ridge Forest General information - Ecoclass concept: The distribution of this ecological site is largely confined to the most recent meander belt of the Mississippi River. The soils that define the site formed in recent sandy alluvium. Within the meander belt environment, these very deep, excessively drained soils are initially deposited as sand splays along levee breaches and on point bars (convex bends) of the river. The geomorphic positions of this site, today, mainly include the high spots of natural levees and meander scroll ridge crests of abandoned river segments that were naturally separated from the main channel prior to construction of the mainline levee system. Additionally, the soils of this site have been mapped locally along a few active tributaries to the Mississippi River. Soil reactions range from moderately acid to moderately alkaline with some pedons exhibiting calcareous characteristics. Slopes of this site generally range from 0 to 5 percent. The natural vegetation of the site is greatly influenced by the frequency of disturbance, depositional environment, and proximity to moisture. Where ample moisture is available, newly formed ridges and splays are largely colonized by sandbar willow (Salix interior), black willow (S. nigra), and eastern cottonwood (Populus deltoides). West of the Mississippi River, the boundary is less distinct except to the northwest where the MLRA abuts the Ozark Plateaus and Ouachita province (MLRAs 116A, 117, and 118A). South of the Ozark and Ouachita escarpment, the MLRA adjoins the Southern Mississippi River Terraces (MLRA 131D), which includes the fabled Grand Prairie and merges with the valleys of the Arkansas and Ouachita rivers (MLRA 131B) and the Red River (MLRA 131C). text: Water features - Water features: This site occupies the highest positions of recent natural levees and meander scroll ridges. The location or position of this site is high enough in elevation that it does not flood on a frequent or predictable basis. Exceptions to this are locations where the soils occur beside or near active tributaries to the Mississippi River. Those locations may receive overland flooding during heavy flood events. This site does not support obligate wetland species or exhibit hydric characteristics.

text: This site is characterized by very deep, excessively drained soils that formed in recent sandy alluvium. A single soil series defines the site, which is the Crevasse (Mixed, thermic Typic Udipsamments) series. Crevasse soils generally form on sandy splays along levee breaks and recently deposited sediments on point bars of the Mississippi River and its tributaries. Reactions of these young soils range from moderately acid to moderately alkaline, and some pedons are calcareous. Slope gradients typically range from 0 to 5 percent. text: Ecological dynamics - Ecological dynamics: Historically, this ecological site was part of a vast forested landscape with processes and functions directly connected to the highly dynamic nature of the Mississippi River (Gardiner and Oliver, 2005). Today, this site is effectively disconnected from the Mississippi River via the vast network of constructed levees and, in many areas, local drainage controls. Widespread changes to the landscape occurred long before any intensive studies of the historic natural communities were conducted. Accordingly, reference conditions of this ecological site are still under review and consideration. This site was primarily created by recent deposits of sandy material on levee breaks (i.e., sand splays) and on point bars of the Mississippi River and its tributaries. These younger deposits are distinguished from their much older sandy counterparts (see site ID: F131AY305MS) by having reactions that range from moderately acid to moderately alkaline and by lacking strata of finer sediments. By their nature, these coarse, excessively drained soils can have severe limitations on plant establishment, productivity, and survivorship. They are normally low in organic matter, available water holding capacity, and natural fertility (USDA-SCS, 1961). Yet, plants and plant communities are capable of establishment where moisture is available.

text: on plant establishment, productivity, and survivorship. They are normally low in organic matter, available water holding capacity, and natural fertility (USDA-SCS, 1961). Yet, plants and plant communities are capable of establishment where moisture is available. Plant communities that develop on this site undergo dramatic changes over time. When these soils are first deposited, early colonizers primarily consist of eastern cottonwood and black willow or sandbar willow, if associated with sandbars and accreting point bars (Eyre, 1980). Although these rapidly permeable soils create limitations for many plant species, eastern cottonwood can survive and is capable of quickly dominating the site and forming even-aged stands (Putnam and Bull, 1932; Johnson and Shropshire, 1983; Hodges, 1997). Notably, stands exhibiting the best growth must have access to some level of moisture during the growing season (Williamson, 1913).

text: site and forming even-aged stands (Putnam and Bull, 1932; Johnson and Shropshire, 1983; Hodges, 1997). Notably, stands exhibiting the best growth must have access to some level of moisture during the growing season (Williamson, 1913). The eastern cottonwood forest type (Society of American Foresters, SAF, Type No. 63) is temporary on this site; it cannot regenerate under shade (Eyre, 1980). Natural “break up” of cottonwood stands may begin as early as 35 years after establishing, but by year 85, stands are transitioning to the next successional community, the eastern riverfront forest association (Meadows and Nowacki, 1996). Components of the succeeding forest typically include American sycamore, pecan, American elm, sugarberry, green ash, silver maple, and boxelder, although cottonwood may continue to persist as a minor component. The cover type generally recognized as representing the riverfront forest in the Mississippi River Valley is the American sycamore – pecan – American elm type, which is a variant of the American sycamore – sweetgum – American elm cover type (Society of American Foresters, SAF, Type No. 94; Eyre, 1980). Since this site, today, occupies abandoned river segments on the protected side of the constructed levee, additional components that are tolerant of these sandy soils may have filtered in including sweetgum and water oak (Quercus nigra).

text: this site, today, occupies abandoned river segments on the protected side of the constructed levee, additional components that are tolerant of these sandy soils may have filtered in including sweetgum and water oak (Quercus nigra). One additional vegetation type may occur on this site in areas consisting of extremely deep sand deposits (dune-like features) that are prone to becoming very dry. These extreme environments are typed as “Mississippi River sandfield mixed herblands” in MMNS (2015). The community is reportedly comprised of a diverse herbaceous layer that is dominated by brome (Bromus sp.), sixweeks fescue (Vulpia octoflora), and pricklypear (Opuntia sp.). Trees may occur but they generally represent a minor part of the community. Woody species reported include Chickasaw plum (Prunus angustifolia), eastern cottonwood, black willow, Hercules’ club (Zanthoxylum clava-herculis), honeylocust (Gleditsia triacanthos), red maple (Acer rubrum), buckthorn bully (Sideroxylon lycioides), green ash, American elm, false indigo bush (Amorpha fruticose), roughleaf dogwood (Cornus drummondii), and possumhaw (Ilex decidua). Overall, natural cover types on this site are minor compared to other uses. Most areas have been cleared and are used extensively for production and other uses. Some areas have been land leveled to meet irrigation needs. A secondary use on this site is pasturage.

text: General information - Ecoclass name: Yazoo - Recent Loamy Natural Levee and Meander Scroll Ridge Forest General information - Ecoclass concept: The distribution of this ecological site is largely confined to the more recent meander belt of the Mississippi River where the soils that define the site formed in recent loamy alluvium. Within the meander belt environment, these very deep, well drained soils were initially deposited on the crests of natural levees and meander scroll ridges. It is critical to note that this site occurs on the protected side of the extensive Mississippi River levee system and is distinguished from similar soils and landforms within the batture lands (i.e., the alluvial land between the river channel and the constructed levee system). Therefore, the geomorphic positions of this site, today, mainly include the high spots of natural levees and meander scroll ridge crests of abandoned river segments (cut-offs) that were naturally separated from the main channel prior to levee construction. Additionally, the soils of this site have been mapped locally along a distributary and a few tributaries to the Mississippi River. The level to gently sloping soils (0 to 5 percent) of this site are of recent origin and lack profile development (Entisols). Soil reaction ranges from slightly acid to moderately alkaline. Colonization of newly formed sites may begin with a heavy stocking of eastern cottonwood followed by the next successional stage, which may consist of sycamore, pecan, American elm, sugarberry, red maple, and boxelder. General information - Mlra notes: The Southern Mississippi River Alluvium (MLRA 131A) is the largest of 4 MLRAs within Land Resource Region O, the Mississippi Delta Cotton and Feed Grains Region. It occurs in portions of 7 states including Louisiana (32 percent), Arkansas (26 percent), Mississippi (26 percent), Missouri (12 percent), Tennessee (3 percent), Kentucky (1 percent), and Illinois (less than 1 percent). The MLRA is comprised of 29,555 square miles and extends roughly 650 miles from an area near Cape Girardeau, Missouri in the north to the MLRA’s transition to the Gulf Coast Marsh (MLRA 151) in the south. Average elevations range from 330 feet in the north to sea level in the southern part of the area.

text: This site is characterized by very deep, well drained soils that formed in recent loamy alluvium. A single soil series is associated with the site in the Yazoo Basin, which is the Robinsonville (coarse-loamy, mixed, superactive, nonacid, thermic Typic Udifluvents) series. Robinsonville soils generally form on the higher positions of natural levees and meander scroll ridges along the current and former channels of the Mississippi River. Reactions of these young soils range from slightly acid to moderately alkaline. Slopes typically range from 0 to 5 percent, which contributes to runoff rates that extend from slow to medium. Permeability of these loamy soils ranges from moderate to moderately rapid. Flooding may be quite common where these soils occur along active tributaries. These areas may experience a seasonal water table that fluctuates between about 4 to 6 feet during the periods of January through April. text: Ecological dynamics - Ecological dynamics: Historically, this ecological site was part of a vast forested landscape with processes and functions directly connected to the highly dynamic nature of the Mississippi River (Gardiner and Oliver, 2005). Today, this site is effectively disconnected from the river via the vast network of constructed levees and, in many areas, local drainage controls. Widespread changes to the landscape occurred long before any intensive studies of the historic natural communities were conducted. Accordingly, reference conditions of this ecological site are still under review. This site was primarily created by recent deposits of loamy material on levee and meander scroll ridges of the Mississippi River and its tributaries. These younger deposits are distinguished from their much older counterparts of long abandoned meander belts (see site ID: F131AY306MS) in having little evidence of pedogenic horizon development and by having nonacid reactions. This soil-site environment has few limitations and is quite productive.

This soil-site environment has few limitations and is quite productive. Plant communities that develop on this site undergo dramatic changes over time. When these soils are first deposited, early colonizers primarily consist of eastern cottonwood and black willow or sandbar willow, if associated with sandbars and accreting point bars (Eyre, 1980). Eastern cottonwood is capable of exceptional growth on these well drained, loamy soils and often rapidly dominates the developing stand (Williamson, 1913). Stands can become very dense and the canopy nearly pure in composition, but the eastern cottonwood forest type (SAF Type No. 63; Eyre, 1980) is temporary on this site. The species does not tolerate competition from weeds, vines, and other woody species and cannot naturally regenerate itself due to extreme shade intolerance (Williamson, 1913; McKnight, 1969; Eyre, 1980; Hodges, 1995). Natural “break up” of cottonwood stands may begin as early as 35 years after establishing, and by year 85, stands are transitioning to the next successional community, the eastern riverfront forest association (Meadows and Nowacki, 1996).
